scenes.visual: Water polarity -> cohesion network, hydration shell around ion, rejection of nonpolar blob
scenes.narration: Water's polarity gives it three jobs in the cell. First, it sticks to itself through a network of hydrogen bonds, which is cohesion. Second, it dissolves charged and polar molecules, wrapping each ion in a hydration shell. Third, and most important for this chapter, it rejects nonpolar molecules, and that rejection is what drives the hydrophobic effect. Water is never just the solvent; it's an active player.
scenes.slideTitle: Three things water does for biochemistry

scenes.visual: Caged water around dispersed nonpolar chips; cluster them; water released; entropy bar
scenes.narration: The hydrophobic effect is the exception that runs this chapter; it's driven by entropy, not by attraction. The second law says a system trends toward disorder. When nonpolar molecules sit alone in water, the water has to freeze into ordered cages around them, which is low entropy and unfavorable. Cluster the nonpolar groups together and you release that caged water back into its free, high-entropy state. The molecules huddle because water gains disorder by pushing them together, and that drives protein folding and membrane assembly.
scenes.slideTitle: The hydrophobic effect: an entropy-driven imperative

scenes.visual: Dance floor: dots moving around wallflowers, wallflowers pushed to corner, floor opens
scenes.narration: Here's a picture for the hydrophobic effect: a crowded dance floor. Scattered wallflowers, isolated nonpolar molecules, force everyone else to navigate around them, and the surrounding water locks into low-entropy cages. Push the wallflowers into one corner and the floor opens up, and the dancers, the water, are free to move. The force isn't attraction between the wallflowers. It's the system maximizing its freedom by getting them out of the way.

scenes.visual: Cone shape -> micelle; cylinder -> bilayer -> closed vesicle (schematic)
scenes.narration: The same entropy that folds proteins builds your membranes. A phospholipid has two greasy tails that water won't wet. A single-tailed molecule is cone-shaped and packs into a sphere, a micelle. But a bulky two-tailed phospholipid is more cylindrical, so it can't form a tidy sphere; instead it lines up tail to tail into a sheet, and that sheet closes into a bilayer that seals itself shut. No enzyme assembles it. Water does, by refusing to touch the tails.
